name: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
title: Storyboarding and Pre-visualization
answer: Storyboarding and pre-visualization cover the planning stage of a moving image project, where shots, camera moves, timing and staging are worked out before principal photography or full rendering begins. In an AI context the term also takes in the generation of concept frames, animatics and camera tests from text prompts, sketches or reference stills. It sits between writing and production, and its output is a plan rather than a finished work.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on image and video generation models, accessed through hosted services or run locally on a workstation with a capable GPU. A typical setup pairs a text to image model for key frames with a video model for motion tests, plus editing or timeline software to assemble an animatic. This site currently tracks 1,000 live image generation models and 1,000 video models, so the practical question for a studio is usually which model to standardise on rather than whether one exists.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A board artist or director starts from the script or a beat sheet, breaks the sequence into shots, and writes or sketches each one. Prompts, reference images and control inputs such as pose or depth guides are used to hold character, wardrobe and framing consistent across frames. Generated stills are then cut into a timed sequence, often with temporary dialogue and sound, so the crew can judge pacing and coverage before committing to a shoot or a full render.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Pre-visualization is where a project's visual identity is fixed, so provenance of reference material matters early. Studios keep records of which images were generated, which were licensed, and which came from a client, because those distinctions shape what can be shown publicly and what can be registered. Style imitation is the live issue: this site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, and a board that closely echoes a living artist or an existing film is a risk carried forward into every later stage.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter integration between boarding tools and the timeline, so a shot list, an animatic and a render queue stay in sync as a sequence changes. Consistency across shots remains the hard problem, and progress there will decide how much of a final frame can be planned rather than shot. The likely split is that pre-visualization becomes faster and more iterative, while human judgement about staging, performance and story stays with the director and the board artist.
